item.title: SAFE Psychological Support Fund opens for applications
item.description:
The Support and Assistance for Free Expression (SAFE) project is now accepting applications for its Psychological Support Fund, open to journalists and media workers in independent media across the Eastern Partnership (EaP). 

Continuous exposure to high-stress and repressive environments takes a profound personal toll on journalists, eroding their psychological endurance and their ability to keep reporting. Through the SAFE Psychological Support Fund, we offer grants of up to €500 to foster resilience and recovery for journalists and media workers in the region. Eligible EaP countries are listed below. 

This support mechanism is designed to allow media workers to access mental healthcare on their own terms, with freedom to choose their preferred care providers.  

SAFE is a project of the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF) under the Hannah Arendt Initiative, supported by the German Federal Foreign Office. The project offers emergency grants for independent media and journalists, covers short-term residencies, equipment support, insurance for journalists on the front lines, provides special support for women journalists and other types of assistance. 

Who can apply 

This call is open to individual journalists and media professionals covering five Eastern Partnership countries: Ukraine, Moldova, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia.

To qualify, applicants must: 

  • Work for an editorially independent media outlet covering at least one of the five target countries listed above.
  • Require psychological support directly linked to their professional duties or working conditions. 
  • Require psychological care that can be accessed within the current programme period. 

What is covered 

The grant provides up to €500 per recipient to cover professional mental health services, including:

  • Individual psychotherapy and clinical counseling
  • Specialised trauma therapy
  • Psychological consultations and psychiatric evaluations
  • Facilitated group support for journalists experiencing work-related stress

Applicants are expected to identify their own, preferred qualified care provider. Treatment may be in-person or remote. 

Application and disbursement timeline

All approved grants are disbursed within the current programme period, until 31 December 2026. Supported services must be completed before this date. 

Application process and deadline

Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis and will remain open until 15 November 2026. We aim to process every request as promptly as possible, though response times may vary depending on the volume of applications we receive.

As part of our review process, we may conduct background verification where necessary. All information shared with us is treated with strict confidentiality and stored in line with data protection standards.

How to apply 

Applications must be submitted in English.

To apply, please fill out the secure application form here.

item.title: The Only Material exhibition comes to Leipzig in October 2026
item.description:
Last year, The Only Material brought the stories of Ukrainian journalists to Berlin. This October, the exhibition continues its journey, this time to Leipzig. On 22 October, we will open The Only Material at the Deutsches Buch- und Schriftmuseum, once again bringing together personal stories of journalists whose lives, work and ambitions have been reshaped by war. It is organised by the ECPMF in partnership with the German Museum of Books and Writing and the organisation Headliner gUG.

Location: Deutsches Buch- und Schriftmuseum (German Museum of Books and Writing), Leipzig

Launch event: 22 October 2026

Doors open at 17:30, start at 18:00

Register here – first-come, first-served: https://forms.gle/HZCHJ17y2MFzsy1c9

Open to public: from 23 October 2026

The Only Material is implemented under the SAFE project, which is part of the Hannah Arendt Initiative and supported by the German Federal Foreign Office. Last year we hosted the exhibition in Berlin. This year it is hosted in Leipzig.

This years’ speakers:

Victoria Yermolaieva is editor-in-chief at Hromadske Radio, a trusted and recognised news source certified by the Journalism Trust Initiative (JTI). Originally from Kerch, Crimea, she was forced to flee due to constant threats and relocated to Kyiv.

Serhii Korovayny is an editorial and portrait photographer whose work has appeared in The Wall Street Journal, National Geographic, and Der Spiegel. A Fulbright Scholar and university instructor in Kyiv, his debut photobook, Love Letter to Donbas, was published in 2026 in collaboration with Fotoevidence.

And last but not least: Diana Delyurman is an independent war correspondent and photographer covering frontline stories, who also serves as Global Communications Manager for the Lviv Media Forum.

For further information visit the exhibition website: https://theonlymaterial.com/

item.title: Slovenia: Authorities urged to refrain from adopting changes that would weaken public media
item.description:
On October 11, Slovenians will vote on a referendum on whether to abolish the licence fee that funds their public broadcaster. In addition, a draft law is moving forward that would give the government decisive influence over the body responsible for appointing the broadcaster’s management.

The undersigned partners of the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR) warn that both proposals risk breaching the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), and call on parliament to pause the legislative process.

Ahead of a consultative referendum on abolishing the mandatory contribution that finances RTV Slovenija (RTV SLO), our organisations stress that removing the existing funding model without a legally binding and adequately protected alternative could undermine the broadcaster’s financial stability and independence.

MFRR partners are also concerned about a separate draft bill published by the Ministry of Culture, which proposes amendments to the RTV Slovenija Act. The new coalition government led by the Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS) is proposing a major overhaul of the broadcaster’s organisational structure.

Our organisations have assessed the proposal and warn that it would concentrate decisive appointment powers within the broadcaster’s supervisory structure in the executive and risks increasing governmental influence over its management and editorial independence.

If passed, the bill would risk reversing progress made since the 2022 reform in strengthening safeguards for RTV SLO’s institutional independence. 

MFRR partners also warn that, if approved in the current form, elements of the proposed reforms would be incompatible with EMFA Article 5, which requires Member States to guarantee the editorial and functional independence of public service media and establishes safeguards concerning the appointment and dismissal of their management and the adequacy, sustainability and predictability of their funding.

The undersigned organisations therefore call on the Slovenian parliament to pause the legislative process and to ensure that any changes to the country’s public media framework are subject to broad parliamentary scrutiny and are developed in cooperation with the public media institutions and their management.

Ahead of the referendum and pending parliamentary debate on the media reform bill, MFRR partners call on the European Commission to closely monitor the situation in Slovenia, including the potential impact of the proposed changes on the independence and sustainable financing of public service media under the EMFA.

The European Commission should assess the compatibility of the Ministry of Culture’s draft bill with the EMFA. The European Parliament’s EMFA Working Group should also make scrutiny of the proposed changes affecting public media in Slovenia a key priority in its monitoring and consultative agenda.

Changes to RTV SLO’s governing structure

On August 26, the Ministry of Culture published draft amendments to the Law on RTV SLO — the first piece of media-related legislation since the Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS) returned to power in the 2026 elections.

The draft law would replace RTV SLO’s current four-member Management Board with a single director general, appointed for a four-year term through a public competition. It would also replace the current five-member Financial Committee with a seven-member Supervisory Council holding significantly expanded powers, including the appointment and dismissal of the director general. As a result, the government would appoint six of the seven members, and RTV SLO employees the seventh.

Under the current law amended under the previous government in 2022, the 17-member RTV SLO Council is composed of six representatives elected by RTV SLO employees and eleven members appointed by a range of independent, public and civil-society institutions. Parliament has no appointment power which fulfills a key EMFA requirement for an independent selection process for the broadcaster’s management. Voters approved those reforms by 62.8% in a 2022 referendum.

As MFRR partners have previously assessed, the 2022 framework strengthened safeguards for RTV SLO’s institutional independence by dispersing appointment powers among employees and public and civil-society institutions, rather than concentrating them in political institutions. The European Commission has also noted positively the post-2022 appointment procedure and its contribution to strengthening RTV SLO’s independence.

The proposed overhaul risks reversing progress and creating serious concerns over its compatibility with the EMFA. Concentrating decisive appointment powers in a single political actor or political majority risks violating EMFA Article 5(2), which requires transparent and open procedures for the appointment and dismissal of public service media management, and requires those procedures to aim to guarantee the independence of public service media. Read together with Article 5(1), which requires public service media providers to be editorially and functionally independent, these safeguards are intended to protect public service media governance from political interference.

The amendments would also terminate the mandates of the current RTV SLO leadership, Council members, and Financial Committee immediately. The premature termination of the mandate of the current Management Board raises particularly serious concerns under Article 5(2), which provides that public service media management may be dismissed before the end of its term only exceptionally where it no longer fulfils the conditions required for the performance of its duties according to criteria laid down in advance at national level. Such decisions must be duly justified, subject to prior notification and include the possibility of judicial review. Automatic termination by legislation risks circumventing these safeguards against politically motivated premature dismissal. The termination of the mandates of the other governing bodies may also raise separate constitutional and rule-of-law concerns.

Changes to RTV SLO funding

In the same bill, the Ministry of Culture proposes removing statutory benchmarks for funding minority programming and music production, while retaining a general state obligation to finance those activities. The change would sever the link between funding for programme-content calls and programmes of special importance and 1% and 3%, respectively, of the annually collected RTV broadcasting fees, in both the RTV Act and the Media Act.

The proposals come as Slovenia prepares to hold the referendum on abolishing the mandatory RTV contribution.. MFRR partners warn that any changes to RTV SLO’s funding model must comply with Article 5(3) of the EMFA, which requires funding based on transparent and objective criteria laid down in advance, and adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.

The referendum frames the choice between scrapping or retaining the mandatory licence fee, without proposing an alternative model. Because it is consultative, the result is not legally binding. However, a strong yes vote would hand the government a mandate to act. The current licence fee model requires citizens to pay €14.02 per household per month.

A separate popular-initiative bill submitted to parliament by National Assembly Speaker Zoran Stevanović, whose party is allied with the ruling coalition, would replace the licence fee with direct state budget financing. It lacks sufficiently strong multiannual and index-linked guarantees, which could increase governmental discretion over RTV SLO’s resources. Parliamentary consideration is expected after the referendum.

Abolishing the licence fee in favour of direct state funding would remove an important buffer protecting RTV SLO’s financial independence.

Additional changes to the Media Act

In addition to the public media law, additional amendments to the Media Act have been proposed by the Ministry of Culture. If passed, the bill would remove or alter existing statutory funding parameters, change eligibility for certain applicants, and alter the conditions for digital media support.

It would no longer specify the amount of funding for media content support, leaving it to the annual state budget, which would give future governments greater discretion over making changes. The provision allowing state media funding to be granted for several years at a time, which lets media outlets plan ahead, hire staff and commit to investigative journalism, would be removed.

Civil society organisations with public interest status in the media field would also lose the possibility of co-financing. The amendments would remove the requirement that a digital outlet must have operated a subscription system for at least one year before a funding call, opening the scheme to fully free online media. 

Wider eligibility can broaden access, but the  requirement currently serves as an objective marker of established outlets with a proven relationship with their audience. Removing it without introducing other clear and transparent eligibility criteria could dilute the funding pool, leave allocation more to discretion, and — combined with annual budget-setting — increase governmental discretion in the distribution of state support.

The Ministry of Culture opened only a short two-week public consultation, largely during the summer holiday period, limiting the opportunity for proper feedback. Any debate on RTV SLO’s future financing and governance must include proper consultations with experts, journalists, and expert civil society organisations. 

MFRR partner organisations remain available to meet the Slovenian authorities to discuss this situation in detail.

  • International Press Institute (IPI)
  • European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF)
  • European Federation of Journalists (EFJ) 
  • Free Press Unlimited (FPU)
  • Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)

This statement was coordinated by the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR), a Europe-wide mechanism which tracks, monitors and responds to violations of press and media freedom in EU Member States and Candidate Countries.

item.title: France mission report: Media freedom at critical juncture ahead of the 2027 presidential election
item.description:
en français

Although France enjoys a legal and regulatory framework which is generally supportive of media freedom, challenges are mounting ahead of the 2027 presidential election,  Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR) concluded in a new report published today. 

The report follows an international press freedom mission to Paris in June, which was led by the European Federation of Journalists (EFJ), and joined by partner organisations of the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR). The mission was also joined by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), EFJ French affiliates (SNJ, SNJ-CGT, CFDT Journalistes and FASAP-FO), and MFRR official partner OFALP.

In recent years, the MFRR consortium and RSF have documented a persistent and growing number of attacks against media professionals. Pressures on media freedom and media pluralism are unfolding against the backdrop of the 2027 presidential elections and in a highly polarised political environment.  

Political deadlock in the parliament and the approaching electoral cycle have stalled key media freedom reforms or fast-tracked them without due democratic consultation. At the same time, growing electoral support for far-right political parties, some of which have demonstrated particular hostility towards journalists, particularly those working for the public broadcaster, raises questions about the future direction of media policy and reform, as well as the protection of journalists’ rights.

The report provides an in-depth analysis of the state of media freedom in the country, following in person and online meetings with journalists, editors, legal experts, civil society organisations, the media regulator Arcom, and government officials including representatives of the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Interior, and the Ministry of Justice. It also examines the state of implementation of EU media laws and outlines key recommendations to reverse the worrying trend.  

The growing concentration in the hands of industrial billionaires, and circumvention of rules regarding internal pluralism, urgent action from the authorities is required to implement the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA). Implementation of EMFA into national law has been stalled, leaving the question of the media regulatory authority Arcom’s regulatory mandate over print and online press unresolved, with no clear timeline for reforms in sight. 

Months following the Parliamentary Commission Inquiry, France’s public service broadcasters have also faced intensified continued political pressure over their funding, governance and perceived impartiality, eroding public trust at a crucial time.

The safety of journalists covering demonstrations is also a particular concern. Journalists covering protests, unrest and politically sensitive events are at risk of violence, particularly at the hands of law enforcement officers, despite being identified as press in most cases. The report addresses the ongoing failure to implement the National Law Enforcement Scheme, the delay in imposing administrative sanctions for police misconduct and the downgrading of the National Plan on Urban Violence to an operational guide that does not recognise the special status of the press. 

Vexatious litigation, including Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs), remains one of the most common tools used to suppress the free press in the country. Although an Anti-SLAPP law was passed in 2026 and covers domestic cases, the law is widely considered to be lacking.

Another pressing issue affecting media freedom in France is the insufficient protection of journalists’ sources. The 2010 law governing source protection contains vague wording and a lack of meaningful standards, and has enabled repeated breaches of press freedom over the past 15 years, including major cases in recent years affecting investigative journalists.

Mission partners also met with journalists in exile from Tunisia, Afghanistan, Benin, Algeria, Guinea, Egypt, Yemen, Pakistan and Haiti, to understand their needs, which ranged from safety to the ability to continue working once they arrived in France. 

Key recommendations to French authorities include:

  • Give full effect to the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), with a particular focus on source protection (Art. 4), public service media independence (Art. 5), and media concentration criteria (Art. 22);
  • Adopt strong anti-monopoly and editorial independence laws for the media;
  • Amend law no. 2010-1 on the Protection of Journalistic Sources with stricter and more clearly defined limitations to the conditions on the lifting of source confidentiality, including independent judicial review ;
  • Amend anti-SLAPP legislation to align with Council of Europe Recommendation on countering the use of SLAPPs;
  • Thoroughly investigate online and offline attacks on journalists to identify perpetrators and held them accountable;
  • Enforce law enforcement officers accountability for attacks against media professionals, and implement the National Law Enforcement Scheme (SNMO) ;
  • Strengthen support to exiled journalists through network building, funding, and language training 
  • Take measures to address transnational repression against journalists residing in France;

The mission report was produced by the European Federation of Journalists (EFJ), ARTICLE 19 Europe, the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF), Free Press Unlimited (FPU), International Press Institute (IPI), and the Osservatorio Balcani e Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT) while RSF contributed to some sections of the report.

  • Adopter des lois fortes contre les monopoles et en faveur de l’indépendance éditoriale des médias ;
  • Modifier la loi n° 2010-1 relative à la protection du secret des sources des journalistes en encadrant de manière plus stricte et plus précise les conditions de levée du secret des sources, y compris par un contrôle judiciaire indépendant ;

en français

Although France enjoys a legal and regulatory framework which is generally supportive of media freedom, challenges are mounting ahead of the 2027 presidential election,  Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR) concluded in a new report published today. 

The report follows an international press freedom mission to Paris in June, which was led by the European Federation of Journalists (EFJ), and joined by partner organisations of the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR). The mission was also joined by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), EFJ French affiliates (SNJ, SNJ-CGT, CFDT Journalistes and FASAP-FO), and MFRR official partner OFALP.

In recent years, the MFRR consortium and RSF have documented a persistent and growing number of attacks against media professionals. Pressures on media freedom and media pluralism are unfolding against the backdrop of the 2027 presidential elections and in a highly polarised political environment.  

Political deadlock in the parliament and the approaching electoral cycle have stalled key media freedom reforms or fast-tracked them without due democratic consultation. At the same time, growing electoral support for far-right political parties, some of which have demonstrated particular hostility towards journalists, particularly those working for the public broadcaster, raises questions about the future direction of media policy and reform, as well as the protection of journalists’ rights.

The report provides an in-depth analysis of the state of media freedom in the country, following in person and online meetings with journalists, editors, legal experts, civil society organisations, the media regulator Arcom, and government officials including representatives of the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Interior, and the Ministry of Justice. It also examines the state of implementation of EU media laws and outlines key recommendations to reverse the worrying trend.  

The growing concentration in the hands of industrial billionaires, and circumvention of rules regarding internal pluralism, urgent action from the authorities is required to implement the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA). Implementation of EMFA into national law has been stalled, leaving the question of the media regulatory authority Arcom’s regulatory mandate over print and online press unresolved, with no clear timeline for reforms in sight. 

Months following the Parliamentary Commission Inquiry, France’s public service broadcasters have also faced intensified continued political pressure over their funding, governance and perceived impartiality, eroding public trust at a crucial time.

The safety of journalists covering demonstrations is also a particular concern. Journalists covering protests, unrest and politically sensitive events are at risk of violence, particularly at the hands of law enforcement officers, despite being identified as press in most cases. The report addresses the ongoing failure to implement the National Law Enforcement Scheme, the delay in imposing administrative sanctions for police misconduct and the downgrading of the National Plan on Urban Violence to an operational guide that does not recognise the special status of the press. 

Vexatious litigation, including Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs), remains one of the most common tools used to suppress the free press in the country. Although an Anti-SLAPP law was passed in 2026 and covers domestic cases, the law is widely considered to be lacking.

Another pressing issue affecting media freedom in France is the insufficient protection of journalists’ sources. The 2010 law governing source protection contains vague wording and a lack of meaningful standards, and has enabled repeated breaches of press freedom over the past 15 years, including major cases in recent years affecting investigative journalists.

Mission partners also met with journalists in exile from Tunisia, Afghanistan, Benin, Algeria, Guinea, Egypt, Yemen, Pakistan and Haiti, to understand their needs, which ranged from safety to the ability to continue working once they arrived in France. 

Key recommendations to French authorities include:

  • Give full effect to the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), with a particular focus on source protection (Art. 4), public service media independence (Art. 5), and media concentration criteria (Art. 22);
  • Adopt strong anti-monopoly and editorial independence laws for the media;

  • Thoroughly investigate online and offline attacks on journalists to identify perpetrators and held them accountable;
  • Enforce law enforcement officers accountability for attacks against media professionals, and implement the National Law Enforcement Scheme (SNMO) ;
  • Strengthen support to exiled journalists through network building, funding, and language training 
  • Take measures to address transnational repression against journalists residing in France;

The mission report was produced by the European Federation of Journalists (EFJ), ARTICLE 19 Europe, the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF), Free Press Unlimited (FPU), International Press Institute (IPI), and the Osservatorio Balcani e Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT) while RSF contributed to some sections of the report.

item.title: Ukraine: One year after Antoni Lallican was killed in the field, MFRR partners demand justice
item.description:
One year after a targeted Russian drone strike killed French freelance photojournalist Antoni Lallican in Ukraine, MFRR partners mark the anniversary by renewing their call for effective cooperation between French and Ukrainian investigations to ensure that justice is secured. The MFRR also extends its condolences to Lallican’s family and stands in solidarity with all journalists working under extraordinary risk in Ukraine.

A Russian first-person view (FPV) drone killed Lallican on October 3, 2025, in a direct strike near the town of Druzhkivka in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk Oblast, around 15km from the front line. He was on a reporting trip with Ukrainian photojournalist George (Heorhii) Ivanchenko. Both were accompanying Ukrainian soldiers on a reporting assignment.

Lallican was killed immediately. Ivanchenko suffered serious injuries and surgeons amputated his leg soon after. One year on, the Ukrainian photojournalist is still recovering and has undergone complex surgery to fit a prosthetic leg.

At the time of the strike, both Lallican and Ivanchenko were wearing protective equipment bearing visible PRESS markings. The targeted use of a drone against a reporting team clearly identifiable as press makes this one of the most shocking examples of a deliberate Russian attack on journalists in Ukraine since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Intentionally directing an attack against civilians is a war crime. The killing of Lallican and serious injury of Ivanchenko must be thoroughly investigated as a suspected war crime, including the evidence that the journalists were deliberately targeted.

The killing highlights Russia’s repeated violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. It is also a tragic reminder of the growing danger facing journalists and reporting teams on the front lines as drone technology spreads. 

The rapid spread of FPV and fibre optic drones, the second of which cannot be jammed, has significantly reshaped the security risks for media working on the front lines by extending the so-called “kill zone.” 

We call on French and Ukrainian prosecutors to provide meaningful updates on the investigations, consistent with their integrity and the protection of witnesses, and to intensify efforts to identify and bring to justice those responsible. French and Ukrainian authorities should strengthen cooperation, preserve and share evidence, and pursue the responsibility of those who carried out or ordered the attack, as well as any commanders whose criminal responsibility is established. Relevant evidence should also be shared with the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, as appropriate.

MFRR partners commend the work done so far by the Temporary Investigative Commission of the Ukrainian Parliament on the Investigation of Crimes Committed by the Russian Federation Against Journalists and Media Workers, which is examining this and other killings of journalists in Ukraine.

Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, MFRR partners have documented 16 journalists killed while reporting in Ukraine on the Mapping Media Freedom database.

The MFRR will continue to document all attacks on journalists by Russian forces and partner organisations will continue to contribute to the Ukrainian Parliament’s Investigative Commission on major cases of impunity. Russia must be held accountable for the killing of Antoni Lallican and for all crimes committed against journalists since the start of its full-scale invasion.

item.title: Malta: Call for a proper review process and international assessment of the media reform bill
item.description:
The Hon. Robert Abela
Prime Minister of Malta

CC: The Hon. Clifton Grima
Minister for Justice, Research and Innovation

Dear Prime Minister Abela,

The undersigned international press freedom and journalists organisations write to you in response to the recent announcement that the long-awaited media reform bill will go before Parliament within the coming weeks.

Our organisations have long engaged in this reform process, including through our submission to the public consultation in 2025. We welcome the government’s stated intention to strengthen protections for journalists and implement EU-mandated reforms, including many of those set out in our proposed National Action Plan on Media Freedom and Journalist Safety.

Ahead of the bill’s tabling, we urge your government to allow sufficient time at the next stage of the legislative process for an open, transparent, and consultative review of the draft, and for legal analysis by national and international stakeholders.

Given the previous involvement of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) in providing legal analyses of Maltese media laws, we urge your government to extend an invitation for review to that body, as well as relevant Council of Europe bodies, to provide expert opinions before the bill is submitted to Parliament.

We recognise the public consultations the government held, which laid the groundwork for this bill. However, that initial consultation on the reform cannot substitute for a broader consultation on the bill’s actual text.

We will contact your office separately to request a meeting on the recommendations in our October 2025 submission. We hope such an exchange will serve as an opportunity to discuss these requests as well as the wider landscape for media freedom in Malta.

Signed by:

  • International Press Institute (IPI)
  • Reporters Without Borders (RSF)
  • Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)
  • European Federation of Journalists (EFJ)
  • European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF)
  • Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)

item.title: Monitoring Briefing 2026
item.description:
The first half of 2026 saw a wide variety of attacks on journalists, media outlets and associated individuals across Europe. item.title: MFRR condemns cyberattack on Mapping Media Freedom
item.description:
The undersigned partners of the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR) condemn the distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack against the Mapping Media Freedom platform on 30 September and 1 October 2026 and express their solidarity with the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF), which operates it.

The attack overwhelmed the platform’s servers and temporarily disrupted public access. ECPMF took technical measures to restore access and the platform was accessible again on 2 October. ECPMF reported the attack to the Leipzig police on 6 October. According to its latest public update, there is no indication that personal data was affected. The source and motive of the attack remain unknown.

Mapping Media Freedom is the platform through which MFRR records press and media freedom violations in the EU Member States and the accession countries. It is managed by ECPMF, but its monitoring is carried out in cooperation with the European Federation of Journalists (EFJ) and International Press Institute (IPI). Its verified alerts help identify recurring threats and patterns across countries, providing an evidence base for monitoring, advocacy and efforts to protect journalists, including practical and legal support. The platform enables journalists, civil society, researchers and policymakers to understand where media freedom is under pressure and what action is needed.

The attack temporarily obstructed access to this public-interest resource. It is a stark reminder of the importance of monitoring violations against journalists and media freedom: the disruption extends beyond the platform itself, interfering with public access to evidence needed for transparency and accountability. Protecting media freedom also requires protecting the organisations and digital infrastructure that document violations and make them visible.

As MFRR partners, we stand with the colleagues maintaining Mapping Media Freedom and contributing to its monitoring. This attack will not deter our joint work to document violations and defend journalists and media workers across Europe.

  • Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)
  • European Federation of Journalists (EFJ)
  • International Press Institute (IPI) 
  • ARTICLE 19 Europe

This statement was coordinated by the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR), a Europe-wide mechanism which tracks, monitors and responds to violations of press and media freedom in EU Member States and Candidate Countries.

item.title: A Bangladeshi journalist, forced into exile: “Staying alive to keep reporting is not a retreat from the profession. It is a condition of it.”
item.description:
In an interview with ECPMF, a Bangladeshi journalist who was forced into exile because of his work spoke about his experiences: what it is like to work as a journalist in a country where press freedom is severely restricted, about the events that forced him into exile and also the psychological impact exile has on him. His experiences illustrate very clearly just how dangerous it is to be a journalist in Bangladesh. For this reason, we will not mention his name in the following in order to protect his privacy. 

By Leonie Hauck

Now being ranked 152nd out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, freedom of expression is severely restricted in Bangladesh. Reporters Without Borders mention Bangladeshi journalists being exposed to police violence, attacks by political activists and murders by Jihadist or criminal organisations. Can you describe what it is like to work as a journalist in a country where press freedom is that much restricted?

The ranking does not define the real scenario; the ground reality is worse. After more than three decades in national and international organisations and media outlets, I have learned that the hardest part is not finding information or drafting a story. For a reporter, a writer or an editor, danger often begins only after the story appears. Secret agencies may block access, seize equipment or delete photographs, mobs or angry crowds may attack the journalist directly, threats follow by phone or on social media and in the most serious cases, criminal actors have killed journalists.

This is not simply my personal impression. According to the Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), 383 journalists were subjected to harassment, attacks or intimidation between January and June 2026, a 32% rise in incidents compared with the same period in 2025. 15 cases filed against 33 journalists under the Cyber Security Act.

A journalist working at district or upazila (sub-district) level does not have the safety that a large newsroom in Dhaka can sometimes offer. Data from July 2026 show that 91% of recorded incidents of journalist abuse occurred at district and upazila level.

Those statistics record the journalists who were attacked, not those who decided not to write or investigate a story at all, not the source who became too frightened to speak, not the editor who quietly removed a story before publication because they anticipated a threat, an attack or a legal case.

The legal environment adds another coat. Bangladesh’s Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and of the press under Article 39, subject to restrictions covering state security, public order, morality, contempt of court and defamation. Such restrictions are not unusual in themselves; what matters is how the laws are actually used. I am not arguing that Bangladesh should have no cyber rule, cybercrime is real, and states have a legitimate responsibility to address it. But journalists need a clear, reliable boundary between genuine cybercrime and legitimate journalism, criticism or public-interest expression.

The problem is now as digital as it is physical. Journalists face hacking, surveillance, doxing and coordinated online abuse, and once a journalist is politically labelled online, harassment can move into the physical world very quickly. A working journalist here has to think about physical, legal and digital security all at once.

Do you have particular examples of challenges you faced?

Yes, unfortunately, I have faced several challenges. The most serious came in 2023 and eventually forced me into exile, but it was not an isolated occurrence. It came after years of professional pressure, questioning, surveillance and intimidation because of my writing, my publications and my work for freedom of expression.

Everything changed in 2023, in two stages, over less than a month. On 14 April, I was invited to a hotel in Dhaka for what I understood to be a meeting about a research project. When I arrived, several unknown men took my phone and forced me away from the hotel area. They accused me of supporting separatists, of meeting indigenous people in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, and of having contacts with foreigners and diplomats. They told me they had been watching me for years. Most importantly, they gave me what they described as a final warning, stop associating with people or organizations they considered anti-national or separatist, and advise me to withdraw from public and critical work altogether. I was explicitly warned not to tell anyone about the encounter.

I took that warning seriously. Discussed with trusted friends, including lawyers and officials of the security and military establishment, tried to find out who was responsible, but could not find out which agency or force was behind it. On 7 May, the day before everything escalated further, I met an Ambassador, who advised me to seek a visa and leave Bangladesh for my safety and security.

The very next day, 8 May 2023, I was abducted. I consider it the worst experience of my life. For the next two or three days I was almost completely cut off from the outside world, physically weak, frightened and unable to think normally. That experience changed my understanding of danger. After it, I understood the danger could become physical, and deadly.

The pressure has also continued in digital form. As a journalist and freedom-of-expression activist, I have faced social-media harassment, defamatory content, hostile online campaigns and attempts to damage my professional reputation, and I have real concerns about surveillance and doxing.

The trauma has not disappeared because I left Bangladesh. I should say plainly that this is not a closed chapter. Nobody was ever identified, nobody was ever held to account, and no investigation was ever opened.

You also engaged as an activist back in Bangladesh. Can you go into detail about that?

For me, journalism and activism were never two separate paths. I started my career in 1995, in a progressive socio-political periodical that dealt with people’s engagement and movements. From the beginning, I was not simply reporting on movements from the outside, but was part of the civic engagement.

By the late 1990s, my work had moved decisively toward grassroots journalism, and this is where most of my activism took concrete institutional form. Working across the coastal region of Bangladesh, I helped build the capacity of local and district-level journalists, usually with no contract, no legal backing and no institutional protection.

I set up a Rural Feature Service to bring stories out of communities that were largely invisible in national media, and I led Jonototthoghar, the People’s Information Centre, in remote areas. The idea was simple: information should flow in two directions. People at the margins should be producers of information, not only its subjects.

That principle led me into advocacy for the Right to Information Act, which Bangladesh adopted in 2009. I believed, and still believe, that access to information is not a technical or administrative matter. It is a precondition for citizenship.

After the so-called “Monsoon Revolution”, which ended the 15 year reign of Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh had an interim government for 18 months. Since the parliamentary elections in February 2026 the Bangladesh Nationalist Party has been in charge. Looking at the political climate of your home country: What concerns do you have in regards to the future of independent journalism?

What worries me is not any single law or any single government. Bangladesh has recently been through three governments: Sheikh Hasina’s own Awami League administration, an eighteen-month interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, and now, since February 2026, the BNP government. That turbulence has produced a climate in which journalists are targeted.

The legal architecture keeps changing its name without changing its character, and this is the part that concerns me most as a long-term structural matter. So when I look at the present government specifically, it is about continuity. Independent journalism in Bangladesh has now survived an autocrat, a mass uprising and an interim government, and people hoped the machinery of repression would be dismantled. Instead, digital surveillance, physical violence, legal persecution, political vendettas, mob intimidation and extremist pressure keep converging into a climate of fear and self-censorship, a structural vulnerability that has outlasted every regime that built a piece of it. The real test for this government, and for whichever government comes after it, is whether that machinery gets taken apart for good, or simply changes hands again. As the IFJ put it in a joint statement with the Federation of Asia-Pacific Journalists and the South Asia Journalists Federation, there can be no resurrection of democracy in this country while journalists remain under threat.

You are very open in talking about struggling with depression. What part does having been forced into exile and separated from your family back in Bangladesh play in that regard?

Yes, I am open about this, because I think it can help anyone living with fear and frustration. Exile did not only take my home from me. It took my daughter and my wife, and that absence sits underneath everything else I deal with here, every single day.

The practical symptoms are real and specific. I have struggled with sleep, and there are days I simply cannot write at all, which is strange and painful to admit for someone who has spent more than thirty years writing. I have experienced memory breaks that unsettle me, and panic attacks that arrive with very little warning, often at the quietest moments.

There was a brief period, in August 2024, when I let myself hope, when Sheikh Hasina’s government fell and part of me thought I might finally go home. That hope did not survive long, and having it taken back was its own kind of loss.

What remains hardest, even now, is the isolation. Therapy has given me real tools, but no session fully answers the simple fact of not being able to hold my daughter or my wife when I need to. I have decided that carrying this honestly, in public, is better than hiding it. Our profession has a culture of endurance, you are supposed to absorb what you witness and keep filing. That culture has a cost, and I think it is time people in this field said so plainly.

Do you have helpful advice for other journalists who are forced into exile?

Exile is a challenge in itself. Try to engage yourself. Stay with journalist networks and continue to produce your own work, even an article, a research paper or a radio script keeps a journalist active and prevents dislocation from one’s whole identity. Build relationships with press-freedom and digital-rights organisations before you need emergency help, not only after. When I needed help in 2023, the organisations that responded (Free Press Unlimited, CPJ, Article 19, Front Line Defenders, and later ifa) were reachable partly because journalism has built those channels over decades.

Take the digital threats seriously from the first day, not after something happens. Exile does not necessarily end surveillance or online harassment, in some cases it intensifies, sometimes onto family members who are still at home. Expect the emotional cost to be real, and not to disappear on any fixed schedule. Seek psychological support early and treat it as a professional necessity, not as a personal weakness.

Journalist organisation desks should document journalists’ suicides, suicide attempts, silent psychological breakdowns and occupational stress, which otherwise remain largely invisible in international press-freedom assessments. Support institutions should establish an independent, confidential, profession-specific monitoring mechanism, while carefully distinguishing verified facts from allegations.

There is one further thing I want to say, because it goes beyond individual advice and speaks to what our institutions owe us. Leaving a country is not a betrayal of the work. A journalist can continue working from elsewhere; it may change shape, but it continues. Staying alive to keep reporting is not a retreat from the profession. It is a condition of it.

As the IFJ put it in a joint statement with the Federation of Asia-Pacific Journalists and the South Asia Journalists Federation, there can be no resurrection of democracy in this country while journalists remain under threat.

You are very open in talking about struggling with depression. What part does having been forced into exile and separated from your family back in Bangladesh play in that regard?

Yes, I am open about this, because I think it can help anyone living with fear and frustration. Exile did not only take my home from me. It took my daughter and my wife, and that absence sits underneath everything else I deal with here, every single day.

The practical symptoms are real and specific. I have struggled with sleep, and there are days I simply cannot write at all, which is strange and painful to admit for someone who has spent more than thirty years writing. I have experienced memory breaks that unsettle me, and panic attacks that arrive with very little warning, often at the quietest moments.

There was a brief period, in August 2024, when I let myself hope, when Sheikh Hasina’s government fell and part of me thought I might finally go home. That hope did not survive long, and having it taken back was its own kind of loss.

What remains hardest, even now, is the isolation. Therapy has given me real tools, but no session fully answers the simple fact of not being able to hold my daughter or my wife when I need to. I have decided that carrying this honestly, in public, is better than hiding it. Our profession has a culture of endurance, you are supposed to absorb what you witness and keep filing. That culture has a cost, and I think it is time people in this field said so plainly.

Do you have helpful advice for other journalists who are forced into exile?

Exile is a challenge in itself. Try to engage yourself. Stay with journalist networks and continue to produce your own work, even an article, a research paper or a radio script keeps a journalist active and prevents dislocation from one’s whole identity. Build relationships with press-freedom and digital-rights organisations before you need emergency help, not only after. When I needed help in 2023, the organisations that responded (Free Press Unlimited, CPJ, Article 19, Front Line Defenders, and later ifa) were reachable partly because journalism has built those channels over decades.

Take the digital threats seriously from the first day, not after something happens. Exile does not necessarily end surveillance or online harassment, in some cases it intensifies, sometimes onto family members who are still at home. Expect the emotional cost to be real, and not to disappear on any fixed schedule. Seek psychological support early and treat it as a professional necessity, not as a personal weakness.

Journalist organisation desks should document journalists’ suicides, suicide attempts, silent psychological breakdowns and occupational stress, which otherwise remain largely invisible in international press-freedom assessments. Support institutions should establish an independent, confidential, profession-specific monitoring mechanism, while carefully distinguishing verified facts from allegations.

There is one further thing I want to say, because it goes beyond individual advice and speaks to what our institutions owe us. Leaving a country is not a betrayal of the work. A journalist can continue working from elsewhere; it may change shape, but it continues. Staying alive to keep reporting is not a retreat from the profession. It is a condition of it.

item.title: Transnational Repression Fact Sheet
item.description:
Many journalists remain at risk even after seeking refuge abroad, facing legal insecurity, professional restrictions, Transnational Repression, and discrimination in host countries. Mapping Media Freedom has recorded 55 attacks against journalists and media outlets living and working in exile in 12 EU Member States and candidate countries from January 2020 to June 2026.

Many of these attacks are forms of Transnational Repression, where state actors seek to intimidate or silence journalists reporting from abroad. This factsheet looks at the different types of attacks and presents case studies of journalists in exile who continue their reporting work aside it all.

item.title: Ein möglicher Austritt Mecklenburg-Vorpommerns aus dem NDR-Staatsvertrag wäre eine Gefahr für die regionale Medienvielfalt
item.description:
Am kommenden Sonntag, den 20. September 2026, findet in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern die Landtagswahl statt. Die Zukunft des öffentlich-rechtlichen Norddeutschen Rundfunks (NDR) ist dabei auch ein Wahlkampfthema der Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). In ihrem Regierungsprogramm kündigt die AfD unter anderem an, den NDR-Staatsvertrag kündigen zu wollen. Zugleich fordert sie die Abschaffung des Rundfunkbeitrags und einen grundlegenden Umbau des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks hin zu einem sogenannten „Grundfunk“.

Ein Austritt Mecklenburg-Vorpommerns aus dem NDR-Staatsvertrag würde nicht unmittelbar zur Auflösung des NDR führen. Der NDR-Staatsvertrag besteht zwischen den vier Ländern Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein. Würde Mecklenburg-Vorpommern den Vertrag kündigen, würde der NDR zunächst in den drei verbleibenden Ländern fortbestehen. 

Das ECPMF warnt jedoch vor den möglichen Konsequenzen einer Kündigung für die regionale Berichterstattung und die Medienvielfalt in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

Der NDR unterhält in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern Regionalstudios in Rostock, Greifswald und Neubrandenburg und das Mecklenburg-Studio in Schwerin. Diese Strukturen ermöglichen eine weitreichende regionale Berichterstattung und versorgen die Bevölkerung unter anderem mit NDR 1 Radio MV und dem Fernsehprogramm „Nordmagazin“. Der NDR selbst weist darauf hin, dass diese regionalen Angebote und Studios ohne den NDR in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern nicht fortbestehen würden.

Die Entwicklung in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern steht dabei im Kontext der jüngsten politischen Entwicklungen in Sachsen-Anhalt. Dort hat die AfD bei der Landtagswahl am 6. September 2026 43,8 Prozent der Stimmen erhalten. Die Partei hatte im Wahlkampf ebenfalls eine Kündigung des MDR-Staatsvertrags angekündigt.

Die politische Situation in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern ist allerdings nicht unmittelbar mit Sachsen-Anhalt vergleichbar. Die AfD liegt in den aktuellen Umfragen zwar vorn, der Abstand zu anderen Parteien ist jedoch deutlich geringer.

Das ECPMF spricht sich ausdrücklich für den Erhalt und den Schutz öffentlich-rechtlicher Strukturen aus. Eine vielfältige und unabhängige Medienlandschaft ist eine wesentliche Voraussetzung für eine informierte Öffentlichkeit und damit für eine funktionierende Demokratie. Weiterhin geht es auch um Medienvielfalt, regionale Öffentlichkeit und die Voraussetzungen für freie Meinungsbildung. Die Bedeutung eines funktionsfähigen öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks ist zudem verfassungsrechtlich verankert. Artikel 5 des Grundgesetzes garantiert die Rundfunkfreiheit. 

Ein Rückzug Mecklenburg-Vorpommerns aus dem NDR-Staatsvertrag könnte den Zugang zu regionaler Berichterstattung erheblich erschweren. Der Schutz dieser Strukturen ist damit auch ein Schutz der Presse- und Rundfunkfreiheit und ein wesentlicher Bestandteil demokratischer Resilienz.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s potential withdrawal from the NDR State Treaty would pose a threat to regional media diversity

This coming Sunday, 20 September 2026, the state election will take place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The future of the public service broadcaster Norddeutscher Rundfunk (NDR) is a central campaign issue for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. In its manifesto, the AfD announces its intention to terminate the NDR State Treaty. At the same time, the party calls for the abolition of the broadcasting licence fee and a fundamental restructuring of public service broadcasting with the introduction of an undefined entity named ‘Grundfunk’.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s withdrawal from the NDR State Treaty would not immediately lead to the dissolution of the NDR. The NDR State Treaty is signed by the four federal states of Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Lower Saxony and Schleswig-Holstein. If Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania were to terminate the treaty, the NDR would initially continue to operate in the three remaining federal states.

However, the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF) warns of the potential consequences of such a termination for regional reporting and media diversity in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the NDR operates four regional studios in Rostock, Greifswald, Neubrandenburg and Schwerin. These facilities enable comprehensive regional coverage and provide the public with popular programmes including NDR 1 Radio MV and the television programme ‘Nordmagazin’. The NDR itself points out that these regional services and studios would not continue to exist in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania without the NDR.

Developments in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania should be seen in the context of recent political developments in Saxony-Anhalt. There, the AfD received 43.8 per cent of the vote in the state election on 6 September 2026. During the election campaign, the party had also announced its intention to terminate the MDR state treaty.

However, the political situation in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is not directly comparable to that in Saxony-Anhalt. Whilst the AfD is currently leading in the polls, the gap between it and other parties is significantly narrower.

ECPMF strongly advocates the preservation and protection of public service broadcasting structures.

A diverse and independent media landscape is an essential prerequisite for an informed public and thus for a functioning democracy. Furthermore, it is also a matter of media diversity, regional public engagement and the conditions necessary for the free formation of opinion. The importance of a functioning public service broadcasting system is also enshrined in the constitution. Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law guarantees freedom of broadcasting.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s withdrawal from the NDR State Treaty could significantly impede access to regional news coverage. Protecting these structures therefore also safeguards freedom of the press and broadcasting and is an essential component of democratic resilience.

item.title: Behind a facade of democracy: A Georgian journalist investigating his own assault
item.description:
Content note: This article deals with police brutality and war.

In 2024, Georgian TV journalist Guram Rogava was attacked during a live broadcast by a police officer – and had to investigate who the attacker was himself. His case illustrates very vividly the state of press freedom in the country. In an interview with ECPMF, he talked about what it is like to be a critical voice in Georgia.

By Leonie Hauck

“It was all live, everyone saw it”, Guram Rogava explains. “I truly believe it was planned because they [the government] wanted some example for others: Look, we are doing this to everyone who has critical questions to us. And please shut up, be silent. If not, you will get the same story.”

The Georgian TV journalist was attacked by a police officer in 2024 whilst reporting live from a street protest in Tbilisi. “He [the police officer] chose me as a target, because I was showcasing to my audience, to my viewers, how police officers reacted to street protests.”

Moments before the attack, a protester had been walking in the direction of the police, holding out his hands to show that he was unarmed. Then, Rogava says, he saw 10-15 officers beating that person really badly. “I was on air, of course I went there, I showed them, and I was saying: Look, look how police officers react to peaceful protest.” Parts of the footage are still available in a CNN report. It shows Rogava backing away and walking towards the sidewalk, when a police officer attacks him from the back. The journalist explains that the policemen had been wearing black masks, black clothes and no identification numbers. “They looked like hooligans, and they acted like criminals.”

Growing up at the border of war

Rogava grew up in this difficult environment for journalists. He describes himself as a rather impulsive person, who is taking dangerous decisions – sometimes without thinking about the consequences. “I live in a country where time is limited and we don´t have a lot of time for planning and thinking a lot about our steps.”

He knew quite early that he wanted to become a journalist. “When I was a kid, in one of the regions of Georgia, it’s called Abkhazia, war started. And my hometown, where I grew up, was at the border of this region.” When the war began in 1992, many of his relatives from this region sought refuge at his family´s home. It was a really hard situation for the whole country, Rogava says. They did not have electricity and there was only a really small room to warm up in winter.

“So we were in this one room, and they [his relatives] were sharing horrible stories about the war, about the crimes, what Russian soldiers did there.” Around 7-8 year old Guram Rogava listened. It was during that time he realized he wanted to tell these stories once he grew up and decided to become a war reporter. He began working in radio as a student. During that time, he covered his first war, when Russia invaded Georgia in 2008. In 2012, he started working as a TV reporter.

Modern Georgia – a hostile environment for journalists

When the attack on him happened in 2024, he was working as a presenter for the Georgian television channel TV Formula. Rogava’s case illustrates very vividly the state of press freedom in the country, which has steadily gotten worse.

In 2025, amendments to Georgia´s defamation legislation were introduced that restricted the protection of freedom of expression. As ARTICLE 19 Europe reported, the amendments included removing safeguards such as the reversal of the burden of proof – thereby shifting responsibilities from the claimant to the defendant.

Then a few months ago, the Georgian parliament adopted a new legislative package criminalising foreign funding and cooperation, which according to the International Press Institute threatens to cut off independent journalism and civil society from important financial support.

The decline in press freedom in Georgia was also reflected in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, published by Reporters Without Borders. Georgia ranks 135th from 180 countries – dropping 21 places in comparison to 2025.

Following the trails of his own case

“After the attack, I investigated my case because the government didn’t investigate it”, Rogava explains. A source gave him information about the masked attacker, but the person was never willing to talk to the journalist. Rogava handed over the evidence he had gathered to the prosecutor’s office on 4 May 2026. However, neither he nor his lawyer had been able to establish the identity of this public prosecutor over the past year and a half. A day later, the journalist broadcasted a special programme on his case together with a colleague.

Then his sources slipped him a letter addressed from the prosecutor’s office to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In essence, it stated: “Please identify the person who attacked Guram Rogava.” The reply came already one day later, saying that they had arrested someone. As he was able to check his official file, he saw that, apart from these two letters, the most recent documents had been added to the file two weeks after the attack. “They just worked for two weeks to collect some papers.” Nothing new had been added in the meantime. “Because one and a half year they did nothing.” 

On 7 May, the prosecutor´s office officially announced the arrest of five persons – one of them supposedly Guram Rogava’s attacker. “We thought, okay, we’ve done our job really well. But it appears they arrested a different person, who was already in jail.” He says they are sure the arrested person is not the attacker. The person that is the attacker according to his sources, remains free.

The future of independent journalism in Georgia

In early August 2026, the journalist had to leave Georgia temporarily. Back home he had been stopped by police officers on several occasions – with no apparent reason. Sometimes when he was in the park with his friends, they started searching their clothes and bags. Or the taxi he was taking was stopped by the police. Rogava feels the authorities are sending a clear message: “We see you, we know you, we know your friends, your family.” He could not bear it if something were to happen to his loved ones, he states.

The journalist emphasises that it is not present enough on an international scale how critical the situation in Georgia is. “Because they still imagine: It’s not Russia. It’s not Belarus. It’s Georgia. Still has some facade of democracy.” But that’s all it is: a facade. “They learned from Russia and Belarus, to do the same things as Putin and Lukashenko do, but with different masks.”

Rogava explains that his colleagues back in Georgia are currently working without pay. He himself is still owed eight months’ salary. As already mentioned, new laws preventing international organisations from helping media in the country financially pose a major problem in this regard. Also more and more companies in Georgia are afraid to book advertisements with critical outlets like TV Formula. “Because if the government sees some company logo on our TV channel, it means this company is bringing money to us. So it automatically means for the government that they are helping us to survive, to continue to ask critical questions.” Sometimes, Rogava adds, they cannot even pay their electricity bills.

To save critical voices in the country, the journalist is sharing his story and raising awareness of the situation in Georgia among international organisations, funders, politicians and the wider public. “It’s really important to have direct communication with people who make decisions. And their one tweet, their one post on social media can be powerful for us because we need to be heard, we need to be seen outside of the country.”

item.description:
4 September 2026

The undersigned partner organisations of the Media Freedom Rapid Response (MFRR) view the upcoming state elections in Saxony-Anhalt with great concern. item.title: Justice delayed, justice denied for Daphne Caruana Galizia
item.description:
European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF) expresses its profound disappointment with the court’s decision to free the alleged mastermind Yorgen Fenech in the brutal assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia. This case is one of the landmark cases in Europe, and we regret that today did not bring justice for Daphne.

The murder of Malta’s most prominent investigative journalist, Daphne Caruana Galizia, on 16 October 2017, was an attack on her, on journalism, and on the rule of law and democracy.

The state failed Daphne twice: it failed to protect her when she was alive, and it failed to ensure justice after she was assassinated. The failure to ensure accountability in her case sends a disturbing message to those who attack and kill journalists.

We particularly regret that Daphne’s family has been denied full justice for their mother, wife, daughter, sister, and loved one. The family has waited almost a decade only to see justice not delivered, and throughout this period they could not rest but had to continue seeking accountability. They had no time to mourn, as the responsibility to fight for justice fell on their shoulders. No family should ever be put in a position where they must advocate for justice themselves.

This ruling is not the end of the story. The Maltese state has an international obligation to hold those who ordered her killing accountable. It also has an obligation to carry forward reforms, including implementing the recommendations of the public inquiry, to ensure no other journalists are killed in Malta and that they can operate freely.

We remember Daphne. We stand with her family. We continue to demand justice.

item.title: Voices of Ukraine expands into SAFE, extending emergency support to media across five countries
item.description:
Since 2022, ECPMF’s Voices of Ukraine programme, under Hannah-Arendt-Initiative, has supported Ukrainian journalists and media outlets. As Russia’s full-scale invasion entered its fifth year, with consequences for independent media rippling beyond Ukraine’s borders, ECPMF is now broadening this work into a new programme Support and Assistance for Free Expression (SAFE) project.

Every component built for Ukraine over the past four years continues under SAFE, and is delivered through the same network of partners behind  Voices of Ukraine, including Public Interest Journalism Lab (PIJL), The Fix Media Foundation, the Association of Independent Regional Press Publishers of Ukraine (AIRPPU), Women in Media (WiM), Lviv Media Forum (LMF), and the Association of Journalists of Kosovo (AJK). Direct emergency grants, the Technology Support Fund, Hostile Environment and Emergency First Aid Training, frontline insurance, dedicated support for women journalists, and short-term residencies in Ukraine all continue as before.

At the same time, SAFE extends the scope of ECPMF’s initial programme to the countries of Eastern Partnership, enabling media professionals in Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine to access three dedicated support funds:

  • Emergency Support Fund:  Financial and safety-related assistance covering  lost or destroyed professional equipment, urgent medical needs, or direct threats.
  • Psychological Support Fund: Grants for urgent mental health support to aid media workers affected by conflict, repression, and hostile environments.
  • Media Capacity Support Fund: Grants to strengthen safety, security, and professional resilience for independent media operating at  high-risk.

This regional expansion addresses a growing media crisis across the Eastern Partnership where locally, political and legal contexts vary but media workers throughout the region face interconnected threats. Independent outlets, already operating under growing pressure, are increasingly struggling against the rollout of restrictive legislation and critical funding cuts. These shortfalls threaten the survival of independent journalism, weakening defense against pervasive disinformation and heightened pressure on press freedom.  

Through SAFE, ECPMF is providing additional places in its existing Journalists-in-Residence (JiR) programme in Leipzig for media workers facing threats or intimidation, offering accommodation, a monthly stipend, health insurance, access to psychosocial support and training.

Opportunities to access support under SAFE are rolling out in phases. The SAFE Media Capacity Support Fund is already active and currently accepting applications for training grants of up to €5,000 per programme, with a submission deadline of 30 September 2026.

To learn more about the full scope of SAFE, visit the SAFE project page. Details regarding eligibility and application steps for Leipzig placements are available on the Journalists-in-Residence page.

item.title: SAFE Media Capacity Support fund opens for applications
item.description:
The Support and Assistance for Free Expression (SAFE) project offers training grants to independent media from the Eastern Partnership region (EaP).

These grants fund training programmes that enhance journalistic reporting and resilience, helping independent media outlets continue their work safely and sustainably under high-risk conditions. 

SAFE is a project of the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF) under the Hannah Arendt Initiative, supported by the German Federal Foreign Office. The project offers emergency grants for independent media and journalists, covers short-term residencies, equipment support, insurance for journalists on the front lines, provides special support for women journalists and other types of assistance.

Who can apply

This call is open to journalists and media workers at independent outlets, whose editorial teams pursue a clear public interest mission and who have limited access to other sources of support.

Priority is given to:

  • Media operating in hostile or restrictive environments: Outlets across the Eastern Partnership region facing significant financial, logistical, legal or security challenges.
  • Frontline and high-risk zones (relevant only for Ukraine): Regional, local, hyperlocal media, small and medium-sized national media outlets operating in frontline areas or relocated from temporarily occupied territories, as well as journalists and fixers regularly working in high-risk zones.

Grants are awarded through a selection process that takes into account the risks and working conditions journalists face in their day-to-day work.

Note: Grants can also be used to fund training for individual members of the editorial team.

How to apply

To apply, please visit this page and fill in the application form. To be considered for the grant, you would also need to download this template, fill it in, and attach it to your application form.

Eligible activities for funding

  • The training programmes must take place before 30 December 2026.
  • The training programmes must target primarily media workers affiliated with the applying media outlet. Eligible topics include, but are not limited to:
    • Mental health
    • Physical safety
    • Digital security
    • Journalistic and editorial skills enhancement
    • Capacity building aimed at improving the outlet’s operational capacity

Grant amount

Up to €5,000 per training programme.

Application guidelines

Applicants must submit a proposal form outlining:

  • Basic information about the applying outlet
  • The purpose of the grant, including the training’s objectives and expected impact 
  • The relevance of the proposed training.
  • A budget, including a breakdown of costs for the proposed training.

Open call deadline

30 September 2026.

Selection process

After an initial eligibility screening, European Centre for Press and Media Freedom (ECPMF) will conduct an evaluation process based on the following criteria:

  • Urgency: How critical and time-sensitive the training is in addressing immediate needs of journalists.
  • Relevance: How well the proposal addresses the specific needs of journalists.
  • Feasibility: Practicality and achievability of the proposed budget and implementation plan.
  • Impact: The training’s potential to improve reporting quality and media resilience. 
  • Sustainability: The training’s lasting impact.

Notification of results

Successful applicants will be notified within 30 days after the proposal deadline.

Grant agreement and contracting

Selected applicants will sign a Grant Agreement outlining the terms and conditions of the grant, including reporting requirements.

Reporting requirements

A report detailing the training outcomes, financial expenditure, and impact must be submitted to ECPMF by 15 January 2027.
